2027 Toyota Crown Signia Gets GT-S Concept Treatment for SEMA, Becomes a Sleek Wagon
25 photos
Photo: Toyota
The 2026 SEMA Show is just around the corner, and automakers are slowly unveiling the vehicles they created specifically for this event. Toyota has already revealed a lineup of five SUVs and trucks with snow tracks , but it will also put a sportier rig on display. Meet the Crown Signia GT-S Concept.
Unveiled for the 2025 model year in North America, the Crown Signia is a mid-size crossover. It's not the bulkiest SUV out there, but it's not exactly sporty-looking either. Well, the GT-S Concept fixes that, turning the Signia into a sleek station wagon.
Built by the Toyota Motorsports Garage, the GT-S Concept looks like its ready to hit the Nürburgring for a few fast laps. For starters, it rides nearly five inches (127 mm) lower than the stock model thanks to a set of custom, one-off MCS (Motion Control Suspension) coilovers.
But the lowered suspension isn't the only feature responsible for the vehicle's car-like appearance. It also rides on motorsport-like 21-inch HRE wheels wrapped in Toyo tires , both of which are tucked under widebody fenders.
Up front, the GT-S Performance Concept flexes a massive grille that puts the Crown Signia almost into Lexus territory. The black side inserts have also grown larger, while the upper thin grille and the badge have red accents (because red makes everything look sportier, right?).
The rear fascia received similar attention, with every single letter finished in red. But the main highlight here is the black diffuser with six vertical fins, flanked by trapezoidal exhaust tips. That's one aggressive-looking rear end! The aero package is rounded off by a pair of vents carved into the upper front fenders.
The slammed crossover is also finished in a custom-mixed dark gray metallic paint with added flake and several coats of clear for extra sheen. It's not the flashiest paint job out there (though it may look better in person), but it certainly fits the motorsport-inspired theme.
Toyota didn't have much to say about the interior, but the images reveal heavily bolstered front seats with red accents and "GT-S" lettering on the headrests. The gear lever also has a red insert for an extra dash of color in an otherwise very black interior.
Toyota had nothing to say about the vehicle's drivetrain but mentioned that stopping power comes from calipers sourced from the Lexus RX 500h F Sport. Needless to say, the GT-S Concept is probably stock otherwise, meaning that it utilizes the same 2.5-liter inline-four engine as the regular Crown Signia.
The mill is paired with two electric motors and delivers a total of 243 horsepower through an eCVT transmission. Toyota offers both hybrid and plug-in hybrid versions , by the way.
Does this concept preview a production model? Well, I wouldn't get my hopes up. The company states that it was put together with "parts and accessories not available from Toyota" and stresses that the modifications "may negatively impact vehicle performance and safety and may not be street legal."
But needless to say, I wouldn't mind seeing a beefed-up version of the Signia in showrooms at some point.

Most electric motorcycles have something in common: a single-speed transmission. But a British company is preparing to shake things up at this year’s EICMA motorcycle show in Milan, where it will unveil a new electric motorcycle demonstrator featuring an unusual two-speed transmission designed to shift gears without interrupting power delivery.
The company behind the technology, E-Motiv Shift Systems , has developed what it calls a seamless powershift transmission, promising improved acceleration, better efficiency, and a more engaging riding experience.
Unlike conventional motorcycle transmissions, which generally require a brief interruption in power during gear changes, E-Motiv’s system is designed to maintain torque throughout the shift.
That could offer some interesting advantages for electric motorcycles, where a lower first gear could provide stronger acceleration while a taller second gear could help optimize motor efficiency at higher speeds.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
Of course, most electric motorcycles don’t actually need multiple gears, and very few have ever offered multi-speed transmissions . Electric motors produce strong torque across a wide operating range, which is why manufacturers generally prefer the simplicity, lower weight, and reduced maintenance of single-speed drivetrains.
But that doesn’t mean a second gear couldn’t offer some benefits.
E-Motiv’s technology actually traces its roots back nearly 25 years to the Zeroshift transmission system, which eventually found its way into Aprilia’s MotoGP racing motorcycles in 2015.
The latest electric version was developed through a £1 million UK government-funded project involving motorcycle manufacturer BSA, the University of Bath, and the Institute of Advanced Automotive Propulsion Systems (IAAPS).
The demonstrator motorcycle, known as Demo 1, was conceived by British design consultancy Envisage and is being built by IAAPS. Real-world testing is scheduled to begin in early 2027.
E-Motiv will showcase the technology at EICMA from November 3-8, though the demonstrator remains a development project rather than a production-ready motorcycle.
Whether two-speed transmissions eventually become common on electric motorcycles remains to be seen. But if E-Motiv can deliver meaningful efficiency and performance improvements without adding too much weight, cost, or complexity, it could give future electric motorcycles another interesting trick up their sleeves.

Eli Lilly’s next-gen weight loss drug retatrutide soundly beat Novo’s approved medicine Ozempic in weight loss and blood sugar reduction, padding the case for a regulatory application that’s expected in the first quarter of 2027.
Eli Lilly’s highly anticipated obesity drug retatrutide—heralded as the strongest weight loss medicine so far—has beaten rival Novo’s Ozempic in a head-to-head Phase 3 test in weight loss and blood sugar reduction, giving doctors a direct comparison as they sort through the many options now, or soon to be, available to them.
In the TRANSCEND-T2D-2 study, both doses of retatrutide—9 mg and 12 mg—reduced average blood sugar (A1C) by 2.2% as compared to 1.8% for Ozempic 2 mg at 80 weeks, Lilly announced Wednesday. As for weight loss, patients taking Lilly’s drug lost an average of 44–47 pounds, representing about 20% of body weight, compared to 21 pounds, or 9%, with Novo’s approved diabetes option.
The study tested the two doses of once-weekly retatrutide in 1,298 adults with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled with metformin, with or without an SGLT2 inhibitor. The main goal of the trial was to show that retatrutide was at least as good as Ozempic in reducing A1C, a measurement of average blood glucose over 2–3 months that is a key biomarker for diabetes. Weight loss served as a key secondary goal.
But while retatrutide had the efficacy edge, the next-gen candidate had a higher rate of adverse events than Ozempic. Lilly reported that 32.7% and 28.3% of patients on the high and low dose, respectively, experienced diarrhea compared with 26.4% for Ozempic. There was also a higher incidence of dysesthesia, a neurological symptom that causes a prickling or burning sensation. The rate of dysesthesia was 4.8% and 6.5% for the low and high doses of retatrutide and 2.7% for Ozempic.
Still, the achievement marks the sixth clinical win for retatrutide, Lilly said in its release. And it was the first time retatrutide was compared head-to-head with another incretin product in a Phase 3 study, according to Kenneth Custer, executive VP and president of Lilly Cardiometabolic Health.
Head-to-head trials are a bold bet from a pharma company, typically reserved for approved medicines to show superiority over rivals. Lilly and Novo have been performing more of these trials as they fight neck-and-neck for dominance of the lucrative obesity and diabetes markets.

“Head-to-head trials show patients and physicians how a potential new medicine compares with treatments that are available and reimbursed today,” Custer said in a statement. “Based on these results and those from across our Phase 3 program, we believe retatrutide, if approved, could shift the treatment paradigm for people living with type 2 diabetes, obesity and related cardiometabolic conditions.”
Retatrutide has generated significant buzz as it nears the market, as well as a black- market for the drug, which is not yet approved anywhere. The Phase 3 TRANSCEND-T2D program, which has enrolled more than 2,050 patients, is helping Lilly build a case for regulators.
Lilly previously reported results from the Phase 3 TRANSCEND-T2D-1 study showing that retatrutide beat placebo at reducing A1C, with an average reduction of 1.7%–2% over 40 weeks compared to a 0.8% average drop for placebo comparators. The drug also elicited weight loss of 16.8% at this timepoint, while placebo comparators saw 2.5% weight loss.
Lilly promised to present more from the TRANSCEND-T2D-2 trial at an upcoming medical meeting.
Retatrutide is the anchor of Lilly’s up-and-coming weight loss portfolio. The injectable triple hormone receptor agonist helps activate the body’s receptors for glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP), glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) and glucagon. The company, which boasts a market cap of $1 trillion thanks to its obesity and diabetes portfolio, has previously announced plans to file retatrutide for FDA approval in the first quarter of 2027.
Lilly is examining the drug for a range of conditions that occur with diabetes and obesity, including knee osteoarthritis pain, moderate-to-severe obstructive sleep apnea, chronic low back pain, cardiovascular outcomes and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease.

The third quarter at C.H. Robinson might be remembered for both the highs and the lows. It was the period when Lipe vs. Lupus Superior came down , and just days after the quarter ended, the giant 3PL announced the almost $6 billion acquisition of rival RXO (NYSE: RXO) .
But neither of those things hit the company’s financial performance, which was strong both sequentially and year-to-year, the latter by a substantial amount.
Operating revenues at its North American Surface Transport unit, which houses its traditional brokerage activities, were up 29.1% from a year ago, with the company citing higher pricing and volume in its truckload and LTL operations. Volume is a particularly important metric at C.H. Robinson (NASDAQ: CHRW) , and benchmarked against the Cass Freight Shipment Index, C.H. Robinson said its volume was up 3.5% year-on-year in the fourth quarter. That contrasts with a small decline in the Cass Index.
Headcount at C.H. Robinson continues to decline. However, the rate of the job cutbacks was slower than in the prior two quarters.
Earnings for $CHRW are out, so let's see how many fewer people work there than before. The rate of reduction slowed. NAST, which houses its brokerage, was down just 1.7% from the prior quarter after 2 quarters of 4%+ reductions. Total headcount was down 2%, lowest since 4Q2024. pic.twitter.com/CCiDGhEYEs — John Kingston (@JohnHKingston) October 28, 2026
The headcount cutbacks have come with improvements in various measures of productivity, which CEO Dave Bozeman referred to in the company’s prepared statement released with the earnings.
“In NAST and Global Forwarding, the team continues to turn manual processes into agentic workflows that are increasingly automated, more connected, and easier to manage at scale,” Bozeman said. “As a result, both businesses delivered a higher level of year-over-year productivity improvements than they achieved in the first half of 2026, and both businesses achieved their mid-cycle operating margin targets again.”
Adjusted gross profit per shipment in truckload was up 17% year-on-year, “despite a significant increase in truckload spot market costs,” with the productivity improvements coming “due to disciplined revenue management,” according to the company statement.
The bottom line was strong, with adjusted diluted earnings per share up 28.6% to $1.80 per share. Adjusted gross profits in the North American Surface Transportation segment, which houses its traditional brokerage activities, were up 16.6% from a year earlier. Income from operations at NAST rose 17.9%. The adjusted operating margin at NAST was up 110 basis points to 40.3%.
With some softening in freight rates there were some negative numbers in sequential comparisons. Revenues at NAST were down 6.16% from the second quarter. But adjusted gross profits were up 10.31%. Income from operations rose 7.43%.
Among the statistics from its trucking activities, C.H. Robinson said the average truckload linehaul rate per mile charged to customers, which does not include fuel, was up 31.5% from a year ago. But costs per mile excluding fuel were up 33.5%, leading to a reduction in gross profits in truckload.
By contrast, LTL’s adjusted gross profits were up 8% from a year ago. C.H. Robinson cited a 4% increase in adjusted gross profit per order and a 3.5% volume increase.
Pre-market trading in C.H. Robinson stock was negative, despite the fact that, according to SeekingAlpha, the non-GAAP EPS of $180 was 5 cents better than consensus forecasts, and revenue of $5.36 billion was better by $450 million.
At approximately 7:50 a.m. EDT, C.H. Robinson was down 4.26% or $6.11 to $137.48. Its 52-week high was $210.33 on July 22, but the Lipe decision has put it under pressure.

JACKSONVILLE, Fla. — U.S. trucking companies could face elevated diesel prices through at least spring 2027, according to energy and truck stop executives speaking Tuesday at the WEX OTR Summit .
Geopolitical conflicts, refinery constraints and limited pipeline capacity continue to strain fuel supplies could continue to impact the trucking industry, according to Chuck Ryan, president and CEO of AMBEST, a nationwide network of independent truck stops and service centers.
Ryan said diesel prices are unlikely to decline significantly before spring, even if global crude oil prices retreat.
“I don’t see it coming down until spring, and that’s if things start to work out on the war front,” Ryan told FreightWaves and Transport Topics during an interview following the panel discussion.
Ryan said the ongoing conflicts involving Iran and Russia’s war in Ukraine have disrupted global energy supplies, while U.S. refining and transportation infrastructure remains constrained.
“If oil dropped today, that does not mean the price will go down,” Ryan said during the panel. “In fact, I think we will have this problem for the next several months, whether the wars end or not.”
The discussion, titled “At the Pump & On the Margin : Navigating Fuel Price Volatility and Network Optimization,” featured executives from AMBEST, Circle K, Maverik and Dow Jones Energy. It was moderated by Will Bowen, senior director of merchant services at WEX.
The second annual WEX OTR Summit was held at the Sawgrass Marriott Golf Resort & Spa and drew more than 115 attendees, including trucking executives, fuel providers, technology companies and other transportation industry representatives.
Panelists discussed how fuel supply disruptions, retail pricing strategies and changing fleet purchasing practices are affecting the trucking industry.
Refinery constraints threaten diesel supplies
Ryan said the nation’s shrinking number of refineries, limited pipeline capacity and changing energy policies have made it increasingly difficult to respond to sudden disruptions in diesel supplies.
The U.S. had more than 300 operating refineries in 1980, compared with approximately 128 today, Ryan said. Although many remaining facilities have expanded their capacity, he argued that the nation’s distribution infrastructure has not kept pace with demand.
“There’s no space in the pipelines. There’s no space in the terminals,” Ryan said. “There’s no place to put additional products.”
Ryan also warned that refineries operating near maximum capacity could become vulnerable to unexpected shutdowns or maintenance problems.
During the separate interview, Ryan said restoring shuttered refineries would require substantial investment and regulatory certainty.
He estimated that rebuilding portions of older California refineries could cost between $1 billion and $1.5 billion, depending on the facilities and equipment involved.
Ryan said major oil companies would likely need to share the financial risks of large-scale refinery redevelopment projects.
Meanwhile, Denton Cinquegrana, director of energy research at Dow Jones Energy, said global diesel markets remain vulnerable to supply disruptions caused by attacks on Russian refineries and shipping restrictions around the Strait of Hormuz.
Cinquegrana said U.S. refineries have been operating above 95% of capacity, leaving limited flexibility if major facilities experience unplanned outages.
He also expressed concerns about refinery maintenance schedules and the potential consequences for fuel supplies heading into 2027.
Winter weather could worsen diesel shortages
Ryan identified the Northeast as a particularly vulnerable region because diesel fuel and heating oil compete for pipeline capacity during periods of cold weather.
“If it gets cold in the northeast, pipeline space is going to be consumed by heating oil, and diesel oil won’t make the line,” Ryan said during the panel. “So then you could get into reliability issues.”
He said trucking fleets should diversify their fuel supply options rather than depend on a single provider.
Ryan said the nation’s refined-product pipelines are already heavily allocated, making alternative transportation methods more expensive.
Transporting additional fuel by truck or marine vessel could help alleviate localized shortages, but those alternatives carry significantly higher costs, he said.
Cinquegrana also warned that the closure of the Philadelphia Energy Solutions refinery following a 2019 fire reduced regional refining capacity, leaving the Northeast more dependent on fuel shipments from other regions.
Even if geopolitical tensions ease, restoring inventories and normal shipping patterns could take several months, he said.
Fleets urged to focus on net fuel prices, not discounts
Beyond supply constraints, panelists emphasized that trucking companies should evaluate the actual price they pay for diesel rather than focus exclusively on advertised fuel discounts.
Meghann Erhart, chief commercial officer at Maverik, said some carriers mistakenly assume that larger discounts automatically translate into lower fuel costs.
She described a customer who shifted purchases to another fuel provider offering a substantially larger discount, only to discover that Maverik’s actual net price was 7.5 cents per gallon lower.
“The depth of that discount could show that you’re buying well and you may be leaving money on the table,” Erhart said.
Ryan agreed that fleets should regularly review their fuel purchasing agreements and understand the differences between cost-plus and retail-minus pricing arrangements.
“If I were a fleet, I would make sure that they get the people in the room who they’re doing business with on a regular basis, not just once a year,” Ryan said.
Rob Nordlander, head of business-to-business commercial sales at Circle K, said trucking companies should also consider the overall value provided by fuel merchants, including reliable equipment, clean facilities and driver services.
He said drivers are less likely to return to truck stops where pumps malfunction, payment transactions fail or facilities are poorly maintained.
The discussion comes as carriers continue to grapple with rising fuel expenses and uncertainty over their ability to recover those costs through fuel surcharges.
AMBEST expanding network amid growing competition
During the separate interview, Ryan said AMBEST expects to add approximately 90 locations in 2026 as the organization expands its network and helps independent operators compete with national truck stop chains.
AMBEST currently has more than 580 branded fuel locations and approximately 120 heavy mechanical service centers, bringing its combined network to nearly 700 locations, Ryan said.
“We’ll grow to 90 this year. And we’ll continue to do that,” Ryan said.
However, he said the organization is being selective about new members to avoid expanding beyond its operational capabilities.
“We’re slowing it down so that we don’t grow beyond our capabilities,” Ryan said.
Founded in 1988 by 25 independent truck stop owners, AMBEST was established to help smaller operators gain purchasing power and compete with larger national chains while retaining their independence.
Ryan said its membership now includes independently owned family businesses as well as operators such as 7-Eleven, Circle K and Casey’s.
The organization has increasingly relied on data analytics to identify network gaps, evaluate customer demand and help members make business decisions.
“That has been probably one of the biggest drivers for our growth, is the ability to bring data to our members,” Ryan said.
He said the independent truck stop sector faces growing competition from convenience store operators and regional fuel retailers investing in high-flow diesel locations.
“The pie is not getting bigger. The demand is what it is, so it’s how much of that share will you have,” Ryan said.
Despite the competitive pressure, Ryan said independent operators can distinguish themselves through customer service, regional offerings and amenities tailored to changing driver preferences.
“Our superpower is the ability to act locally,” he said.
During the panel, Ryan also urged independent truck stop owners to modernize their facilities rather than rely on business models and amenities designed decades ago.
“You have to operate a truck stop like it should in 2026, not in the previous century,” Ryan said.
Ryan, whose father worked as a truck driver, said the industry’s long-term success ultimately depends on recognizing the importance of drivers and providing services that meet their needs.
“There’s nothing in this room, there’s nothing you do or I do that doesn’t involve a truck,” Ryan said.
Why it matters: Energy and truck stop officials said prolonged diesel price volatility could add financial pressure to trucking companies already struggling with rising operating costs.

The DM Vans LV7 Backcountry Is a Spacious Camper Van That Makes Everyday Routines More Comfortable
20 photos
Photo: DM Vans
Some people argue that van life is losing its appeal, with many travelers moving away from life on the road and returning to traditional homes. But a quick search on social media under the van life hashtag suggests otherwise. The van life trend is still going strong, and interest in camper vans continues to inspire new builds.
If anything, more van conversion companies are emerging to meet the increasing demand, offering well-equipped rigs for everything from weekend escapes to full-time van living. One of the latest manufacturers to catch my attention is DM Vans, a boutique Colorado-based shop that has been building custom camper vans based on the RAM ProMaster chassis since 2018.
The company was founded by two experienced van lifers who wanted to help others fulfill their travel dreams, and they use their firsthand knowledge of life on the road to create practical roving homes . They call their rigs “Class B Lifestyle Vehicles” and have completed over 800 custom builds so far.
Their offering includes three models - the LV3 aimed at weekend warriors or solo travelers, the LV5 for couples seeking more than a camper, and the LV7 designed for extended trips or full-time use. Each is manufactured to RVIA standards, with high-quality materials, excellent craftsmanship, and great attention to detail.
Photo: DM Vans Built on the RAM ProMaster 159-inch Extended SLT chassis, the 2027 LV7 Backcountry is the company’s most capable and complete conversion aimed at people who are serious about van living . It combines a reliable platform with a spacious interior designed to deliver an upgraded mobile living experience, plus an electrical system that enables extended off-grid adventures.
With maximum cargo volume, generous headroom, and a square interior geometry, the RAM ProMaster provides a great base for this conversion. Not to mention, it comes with a range of handy driver-assistance features, including Full-Speed Forward-Collision Warning, Blind-Spot and Cross-Path Detection, and Active Driving Assist.
Finished in dark granite gray, the van conversion featured in the photos and the video below is a rather unassuming build, with very few details that point to its camper identity. The most obvious one is the full-length roof rack, which has become standard equipment for the 2027 model year.
Photo: DM Vans DM Vans added this feature to give owners extra space for carrying gear and the possibility to configure the top of the van as they please with fewer holes in the roof. The rack is compatible with most awnings on the market, and an optional side ladder attaches directly to it for easier roof access.
For LV7 Backcountry’s interior, the outfitter focused on space efficiency. They used the 463 cubic feet of living space to include a full kitchen, a comfortable raised bed, seating and dining space, and smart storage designed for extended living. At the front, they kept the floor plan open, with no divider wall behind the driver’s and passenger’s seats, which are also swivel seats, so they become part of the living space at camp.
Style-wise, DM Vans went for a modern, minimalist design with a bright Scandinavian-inspired aesthetic. White cabinetry with flat, handleless cabinet faces and flush-mounted drawers gives the interior a clean look, while natural wood countertops and a stained tongue-and-groove ceiling add a bit of warmth and texture.
The white-dominated color scheme might not be to everyone’s taste, but it definitely helps make the interior feel open and uncluttered.
Photo: DM Vans The kitchen runs along the driver’s side of the van and is equipped with an induction cooktop, a sink, and a 12-volt compressor fridge. Instead of the typical backsplash, the LV7 features a nifty wooden shelf that is perfect for keeping utensils or spices easily accessible. An opening window above the counter is another nice touch, allowing for nice views and improved ventilation while cooking.
A seating arrangement is included nearby, with a long bench along the passenger side and a smaller one next to the kitchenette. Apart from seating, these upholstered benches double as storage and as steps leading to the elevated rear bed. A versatile Lagun table slides out from under the bed. You can position it however you like to use it for dining or working, and when you don’t need it anymore, it neatly stows away, opening up the floor space. A Trelino composting toilet is stored inside the smaller cube.
For the sleeping arrangements, buyers can choose between a short king bed or a full-size bed with a full-height wardrobe beside it, as shown in the video. The wardrobe is a really nice addition for those living in their vans full-time, as it offers ample storage for clothes and personal belongings. The storage options in this conversion also include upper cabinets, an open bungee shelf, a multi-functional storage unit above the bed, and rear door organizers.
Photo: DM Vans But the largest storage compartment is the open garage area under the bed. Built-in side cabinets hold the van’s systems, while the central area is perfect for larger items or bulky equipment. What’s more, the floor of this garage is carpeted, so it doesn’t look too utilitarian.
But one of LV7 Backcountry’s strongest suits is its electrical system, which is perfectly capable of handling long off-grid journeys. It includes a 1,200Ah lithium battery bank (four 300Ah batteries) with a stated capacity of 14.4 kWh, two 200-watt solar panels, dual 50-amp DC-to-DC chargers with MPPT solar controllers, and a 3,000-watt inverter.
The water system, on the other hand, is not so impressive, as the van only carries 7 gallons (26 liters) of fresh water and 7 gallons of gray. The good part, though, is that the tanks are easy to replenish and the sink has an accumulator that allows you to control the water flow.
The van is also equipped with a Peak Heating System and reversible front and rear ventilation fans, plus a high-efficiency 12-volt AC unit, giving you multiple ways to manage airflow and interior temperature.
Photo: DM Vans DM Vans offers a list of optional upgrades as well, including an L-track system for the garage area, additional Lagun tables, reflective interior window covers, running boards, a spare tire carrier, all-terrain tires, and traction boards. Bug nets and an external Starlink port are also available, and buyers can also extend their off-grid setup with more solar and battery capacity.
The 2027 DM Vans LV7 Backcountry camper van is now available for pre-order, with a starting price of $124,800. Deliveries are scheduled to begin in early November.

source_document.body:
Nearly 35,700 import containers were waiting for on-dock trains at the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach this week, as record cargo volumes and reported railcar shortages slowed the movement of freight inland.
Of the 35,688 containers awaiting rail service on Oct. 26, 10,562 had been on the terminals for at least nine days, according to The Dwell’s compilation of the ports’ daily rail reports. The figures count individual containers, rather than twenty-foot-equivalent units, or TEUs, the standard measure of port cargo volume.
The backlog was more severe at Los Angeles, where 8,133 of the 19,626 containers awaiting trains had waited nine days or longer. At Long Beach, 2,429 of 16,062 rail-bound containers had reached that threshold. That put the share of longer-waiting containers at 41.4% in Los Angeles, compared with 15.1% in Long Beach.
The daily inventory figures follow a broader increase in the time containers spend on marine terminals. Average rail-container dwell across the port complex rose to 7.19 days in September from 6.75 days in August, according to Pacific Merchant Shipping Association data. Average dwell for containers leaving by local truck increased to 3.18 days from 2.95 days.
Both ports handled record monthly cargo volumes in September. Los Angeles processed approximately 1.04 million TEUs, while Long Beach handled 997,177 TEUs. PMSA linked the increase in container dwell to the extended peak shipping season and heavy cargo flows.
Freight broker C.H. Robinson identified Southern California intermodal railcar shortages as a constraint in its October market update, saying limited equipment availability was extending import dwell and slowing inland movement. Empty-container repositioning was also complicating equipment flows, while truck-destined containers were moving relatively normally by comparison.
The figures point to particular pressure on the rail side of the ports’ operations. The Oct. 26 counts measure containers awaiting on-dock trains at a particular moment; they are not an average waiting time and do not establish that every container in the inventory is overdue.
Class I railroads BNSF (NYSE: BRK-B ) and Union Pacific (NYSE: UNP ) serve the southern California port complex.
“Strong international volumes have tightened rail car supply, but Union Pacific’s buffer resources have positioned us well to maintain fluidity throughout the extended international peak,” a UP spokesperson said in an email statement to FreightWaves. “Strong westbound volumes are also supporting car supply. We continue to pull consistently from the docks and leverage our ICTF facility to keep freight moving, while maintaining the car supply needed to support fluid port operations.”
Port of Los Angeles Executive Director Gene Seroka is scheduled to speak with FreightWaves later Wednesday. FreightWaves has also reached out for comment from the Port of Long Beach and BNSF.
The buildup of containers on terminals has not been accompanied by evidence of a comparable offshore vessel queue. The Dwell’s separate congestion tracker reported one ship awaiting a berth during the week of Oct. 26, based on Maritime Administration and Marine Exchange data.
A possible labor disruption could add pressure in the coming days. The Pacific Maritime Association warned Oct. 27 that a potential Nov. 1 strike involving approximately 250 port watchmen could affect eight container terminals. Members of International Longshore and Warehouse Union (ILWU) Local 26 voted to approve a walkout as soon as Sunday.
According to the employer association, the terminals handle roughly 85% of Long Beach cargo and 33% of Los Angeles cargo.
This article was updated on Oct. 28 to add comments from Union Pacific.

Biogen is growing as planned, with marketed products generating more revenue and multiple late-stage readouts expected over the next year. Building out an early-stage pipeline would be a bonus, CEO Chris Viehbacher said on a Q3 earnings call Wednesday.
After three straight quarters of rising revenue thanks to existing products, Biogen now sees its carefully crafted late-stage pipeline as icing on the cake, with deals another nice to have but not necessary sprinkle on top.
“Given the Apellis acquisition, we now think that the company can grow even without the pipeline,” CEO Chris Viehbacher said on a Wednesday morning earnings call. “So as the pipeline starts to read out . . . we’ll be able to launch products on top of a growing base.”
Growth was certainly the topic du jour during Biogen’s third-quarter earnings report—with some variation of the word spoken 48 times on the call by the company executives or analysts eager to understand their strategy.
That growth was generated by increasing sales of Alzheimer’s disease therapy Leqembi and spinal muscular atrophy antisense oligonucleotide Spinraza, as well as the products Biogen acquired in its $5.6 billion Apellis Pharmaceuticals buy in March.

Now, the company is looking to three key pipeline products: litifilimab in two types of lupus, felzartamab in antibody-mediated rejection (AMR) and zorevunersen for Dravet syndrome. Biogen has key registrational readouts for litifilimab coming in the next four quarters: Two Phase 3 readouts in systemic lupus erythematosus are expected first, by the end of this year, followed by a late-stage readout in cutaneous lupus erythematosus in the first half of 2027.
With these trials poised to deliver data that could launch meaningful products, Viehbacher said the company will stay focused on developing internal programs while watching for potential early-stage business development opportunities.
“Investors have waited a long time for us to grow, and so we’re going to be very mindful of different ratios and the amount of investment versus growing our bottom line,” the CEO said. “But I think we can manage all of that actually.”
Apellis was a late-stage addition, adding two approved medicines in kidney and eye disease. Viehbacher reiterated his preference for earlier-stage acquisitions going forward.
“I’ve really always hated having to go buy assets in later stage because there’s still a fair amount of risk associated with that,” Viehbacher said. “If we have reasonable success with the pipeline—again we have to wait and see the results—but there’s a good potential that the company can just grow now for the foreseeable future.”
Viehbacher said that assets in the discovery stage to Phase 1b that can fit into Biogen’s existing franchises are the company’s “sweet spot” as they have become more opportunistic than intentional about deals.
“One of the things I’m quite mindful of is distraction. We have dramatically changed at Biogen,” Viehbacher said. While just a few years ago the company was pitching its therapies solely to neurologists, Biogen’s commercial teams are now working with nephrologists, dermatologists, retina specialists and rheumatologists across the product portfolio.
“All of that is a tremendous amount of change, and I think we really want to be able to digest that change and really take advantage of the opportunities that are in front of us and be careful about overextending ourselves,” the CEO said.

By Alexander Whiteman
28 October 2026
Seko logistics is urging shippers sourcing from China to bring forward purchase orders and confirm ocean bookings at least four weeks ahead of shipment, as an earlier lunar new year in 2027 threatens to compress the window for moving cargo before factory closures.
Falling 11 days earlier than in 2026, next year’s holiday starts on 6 February, and Seko MD for the UK and Ireland Paul Lockwood told The Loadstar : “We are already seeing customers adjust critical path planning to bring their ex-factory dates forward to allow for the earlier lunar new year.
“One customer has advised they raised their purchase order with their suppliers three weeks before the typical purchase order date to account for this, and to ensure they are not ‘back of the queue’ in the production cycle.”
The move reflects growing concern that orders placed too late could miss pre-holiday shipping windows and face delays as exporters compete for capacity, shippers already battling disruption across Asian container networks.
Analysis from Sea-Intelligence found vessel delays, caused by typhoons and port disruption, had absorbed around 3m teu of global container capacity, equivalent to 8.5% of the total, compared with a 2011-19 average of 2.2%.
“At the same time, ocean carriers typically introduce additional blanked sailings around the lunar new year period, while exporters concentrate shipments into the weeks immediately before the holiday,” a spokesperson for Seko’s China office told The Loadstar .
“This makes the pre-holiday period one of the busiest times of the year for China’s exports. We therefore recommend placing bookings at least four weeks in advance and building sufficient time into factory completion, origin collection and port delivery plans.”
The spokesperson noted that relatively few factories had formally announced their 2027 holiday schedules, but existing plans indicated that production shutdowns would vary by region, with those Seko works with in northern China planning a 25 January-15 February shutdown.
However, local practices in some regions often see manufacturers beginning the holiday period up to a week ahead of the spring festival and not fully resuming operations until after the Lantern Festival on 20 February.
In southern China, the downtime is expected to be even longer, with some operators set to shut down three weeks ahead of the festivities and not be back up to full production for a fortnight after the holiday.
Seko Logistics’ client solutions group director for the UK & Ireland, Dan Eckett, said: “Ocean freight is heavily impacted in the weeks leading up to the new year, as exporters accelerate shipments ahead of factory closures.
“This creates pressure on vessel space, equipment availability and carrier schedules, so we typically recommend building an additional one to two weeks into transit plans and ensuring supplier bookings are confirmed well before that three-week threshold, not after it.”
For UK importers, this means production completion dates and port cutoffs must be worked backwards from the intended sailing, with contingency built in for delays at origin, if they are to avoid the viable albeit economically questionable airfreight and sea-air services.

Nearly half of the supply chain organizations in a Gartner survey reduced headcount primarily because of AI over the past two years, with those organizations reporting an average reduction of 10.5%. Entry-level employees have been especially affected as companies change how work gets done.
What’s Related
Gartner found that 47% of the supply chains surveyed had cut staff primarily due to AI. Separately, 66% of leaders reported a decline in entry-level headcount, more than double the share reporting reductions at other levels.
The findings come from organizations that already use AI in their workflows to some degree. They do not represent a survey of the entire supply chain industry.
“AI is thinning the entry-level supply chain workforce faster than most chief supply chain officers (CSCOs) are redesigning the talent pipeline, creating a future capability gap that will actually weaken their organizations’ AI performance,” said Tess Frenzel, Director Analyst in Gartner’s Supply Chain practice.
Fewer new hires, fewer future leaders
Gartner said cutting entry-level hiring without changing what those employees do could leave companies with fewer people prepared to move into senior positions. Supply chains have traditionally relied on a large pool of junior employees to develop future leaders, even when many leave along the way.
A smaller incoming group makes hiring, training, and retaining promising employees more important. At the same time, Gartner found that expectations for middle-management skills have changed compared with two years ago.
“Producing fewer candidates for traditionally defined leadership roles is a miscalculation, as supply chains will require new competencies both for entry-level and leadership positions as a result of working alongside AI,” Frenzel said.
RELATED STORIES: Eight Ways AI is Transforming the Modern Warehouse | Six Supply Chain AI Developments Worth Watching
Changing the entry-level job
Gartner’s analysis found that its highest-performing supply chains are raising expectations for entry-level employees. The firm defined that group as the top 25% based on AI integration, AI-enabled automation , and business outcomes.
“Compared with two years ago, these organizations require more domain-specific and analytics skills and greater supply chain experience, while involving entry-level employees in less repetitive work and more consequential decisions,” Frenzel said.
Gartner recommends three steps to help supply chain leaders prepare junior employees for more demanding roles:
Pair junior employees with experienced colleagues. Match technically skilled entry-level employees with mid- and senior-level staff to build business knowledge while helping deploy and oversee AI.
Make responsibility for AI clear. Track AI usage, regularly test the data and assumptions behind its models, and assign clear accountability for results.
Build teams across supply chain functions. Bring employees from different areas together to share knowledge and work toward common performance goals.

The Koa Is an Off-Grid-Ready Camper Van With a Striking Walnut and Maple Interior Design
20 photos
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / Beachside Custom Vans
If you come up with the right layout and design, you can make a camper van almost as comfortable as a simple studio apartment. Today, I have just the right camper van to share with you to prove what I just said.
Meet Koa, a conversion based on a 2026 AWD Mercedes-Benz Sprinter with a 144" wheelbase and a high roof. It's the work of Beachside Custom Vans, a Jacksonville, Florida-based boutique camper van builder specializing in roam-ready mobile homes.
This Sprinter doesn't have that many exterior upgrades like we've seen on other vans. However, the ones it does have make it relatively obvious that you're looking at a camper .
For instance, a ladder on the driver's side offers quick and easy access to the roof. There, you'll come across a White Top Adventure rack that holds a 200 W solar panel. The roof also has a ProBreeze vent fan and a Victron A/C unit.
Beachside Custom Vans gets standard cargo vans from Mercedes, which come with no windows. The company adds them itself – this rig has two AM Auto half-slider windows, as well as two windows at the back.
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / Beachside Custom Vans Other notable mods are Dark Star Offroad side steps, power and water hookup points, and a set of flares.
Flares, also known as pods or capsules, are designed to increase the van width to allow you to fit a bed inside in an east to west arrangement instead of the standard north to south. This rig's fiberglass pods are finished in black, and the one on the passenger side has a half-slider window.
Inside is where the biggest transformation happened. Slide the door open, and a beautifully designed interior will greet you. It has an open layout, with no wall separating the driver's cabin from the living space. Moreover, the driver and passenger seats are mounted on factory swivel bases, so they can be turned around to face the back of the van.
Regarding aesthetics, the customer opted for Lonseal walnut and holly marine-grade vinyl flooring, wall panels upholstered in Marathon Plus oat-colored woven fabric, a matching ceiling, and a mix of maple and walnut cabinetry: maple for the lowers and walnut for the uppers. The look is completed by white solid surface countertops and three lighting zones.
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / Beachside Custom Vans Straight ahead as you enter, Beachside Custom Vans devised a single-person bench with a Lagun table mount. It offers a bit of storage space in the form of a cabinet with two shelves.
Next, we have the kitchen, which is split into two units. It features a Dometic NRX 115 fridge with a tiny freezer compartment, a humongous stainless steel sink with a cover that matches the countertop, a portable single-burner induction stove, a 4-in-1 oven, and a flip-up table that offers additional surface area. A ProBreeze vent fan is perfectly positioned above to draw out the smells and fumes from cooking.
Two overhead cabinets, a cutlery drawer, and two lower cabinets are available for storage in the kitchen. There's also a floor-to-ceiling unit on the driver's side that integrates a closet with hanging space, as well as three drawers.
The drawer on the bottom hides a Laveo dry-flush toilet – since the drawer has heavy-duty slides, you don't have to remove the toilet to use it. Just sit down and get to business.
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / Beachside Custom Vans In the rear, you get a fixed sleeping arrangement. It boasts a queen-size bed, three overhead cabinets, charging points, and a ceiling A/C unit.
Finally, the space underneath the bedroom serves as a garage. To make loading and unloading items easier, the builders added a pull-out tray attached to heavy-duty slides. They can support up to 500 lb. (227 kg).
The garage's sides are taken up by large boxes that accommodate the utility systems. Power is on the left side – the electrical system's highlights are two 200 Ah lithium batteries and a 3,000 W inverter.
Three charging sources can be used to keep the batteries topped off: solar power , shore power, and 50-amp DC-DC charging while the engine is running. If used right, you'll never run out of juice. Furthermore, a temperature sensor detects if the electrical box gets too hot, and turns on two fans (one on each end) to pump out the hot air.
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / Beachside Custom Vans As for plumbing, the van is equipped with a 35-gallon (132-liter) freshwater tank, an 11-gallon (41-liter) greywater tank with an electronic dump valve, a 4-gallon (15-liter) water heater, and an outdoor shower connection.
The "command center" for the rig's utilities is conveniently located in the kitchen, integrated into the side of the floor-to-ceiling unit I mentioned earlier. It includes standard and USB outlets, three dimmer light switches, a touchscreen display for monitoring power and water, and switches for the water system.
All in all, the Koa packs all most people need to hit the road in comfort and style. The cherry on top is that the rig can keep its occupants on the road for longer periods thanks to its off-grid-ready setup. By the way, this van is built on the company's Drifter model, but it has a few additions.
As mentioned in the title, Koa is looking for a new owner. According to the listing by Beachside Custom Vans , its price tag is $144,500 (€129,240). The vehicle has just 400 miles (644 km), which is basically brand-new for a camper van. The company also offers a 2-year Beachside builder warranty.

LONDON — Finance minister John Healey said on Wednesday “reprioritization” in other departments would fill a £4.7 billion ($6.3 billion) gap in Britain’s Defence Investment Plan, a blueprint government hopes shows its NATO commitment .
In his first budget, Healey said he would also adopt this approach of “looking hard at public spending” to set out the details of how Britain will meet the NATO commitment of spending 3.5% of GDP on defense by 2035, and mark a target date for 3% in 2030.
“In today’s budget, I am fully funding the Defence Investment Plan, including through capital reprioritization across Whitehall. This honors the commitment made both by me – and by the prime minister,” he told parliament, referring to a part of London home to most government departments.
Healey, Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Defense Minister Wes Streeting are under pressure to increase investment more quickly.
Confirming that detailed plans for reaching the 3% and 3.5% goals will be set out in a spending review planned next year, Healey said he was also “determined to use more innovative financing, alongside the private sector and our international allies.”
That delay in plotting a clear pathway to 3.5% will heighten calls by the main opposition Conservatives, who have demanded Healey’s resignation if he failed to set out a credible plan at the budget.
Healey resigned as defense minister under Keir Starmer in June over what Healey viewed as inadequate spending on defense, specifically over the former prime minister’s unwillingness or inability to find funds to reach the 3% goal by 2030.

With pressure on GSK’s vaccine business, analysts predict the U.K. pharma will face challenges as it prepares for the loss of exclusivity on a key product.
GSK recorded flat-to-falling sales at its cornerstone vaccine and general medicine businesses in the third quarter, leading analysts to predict the company will face challenges as it tries to expand in oncology.
The pharma reported Wednesday that it clocked overall sales at £8.9 billion ($11.83 billion)—in line with consensus estimates, Guggenheim Securities analysts said in a note to investors. However, vaccine sales fell and missed expectations, landing at £2.6 billion ($3.46 billion). The general medicine unit beat expectations, notching £2.4 billion ($3.19 billion), but revenues were flat. GSK is pivoting to specialty medicines, where sales increased 15% to £3.9 billion ($5.18 billion) at a constant exchange rate, but analysts see the quarter as evidence the transition could be difficult.
“Net-net, while we understand the push into oncology, we believe this quarter highlights the challenges of delivering sustainable growth in the face of large and relatively flat vaccines and [general medicines] businesses as we approach dolutegravir’s patent expiry,” Guggenheim analysts said. Dolutegravir is an HIV drug that will lose exclusivity toward the end of the decade.
Sales of the respiratory syncytial virus vaccine Arexvy fell more than 20%, which GSK partly attributed to lower market demand. At £195 million ($259 million), Arexvy sales missed the consensus expectation of £231 million ($307 million). GSK’s shingles vaccine, Shingrix, also underperformed expectations, falling 5% on a constant-currency basis against a backdrop of market pressures.
“The . . . adult vaccines market overall is still challenging,” GSK CEO Luke Miels said on a Wednesday earnings call. “Shingrix is doing a little bit better in relative terms. The adult market is down about 18% versus this time last year, but Shingrix is down about 14%.”
The launches of Blenrep in multiple myeloma and Exdensur in asthma “continue to ramp slowly,” Guggenheim said. At £50 million ($66 million), sales of the antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) Blenrep met analyst expectations. Exdensur fell short, generating £27 million ($36 million) versus the £36 million ($48 million) consensus.
Miels highlighted both products. GSK “made good progress on Blenrep, where repeat prescribers are growing as physicians and patients get comfortable using the medicine,” the CEO said. He added that Exdensur is building momentum, “with prescribers, patients and access all increasing in the quarter.”
The situation means the launches of Hibsago in chronic hepatitis B and Jideytro in ROS1-positive non-small cell lung cancer are “increasingly critical,” the analysts said. The products will “meaningfully contribute to near-term growth,” Miels said. Hibsago, which the FDA approved last week, will be on the market within 10 days, Nina Mojas, president of global product strategy at GSK, said on the earnings call.

The 2026 SEMA Show continues the tradition of the annual automotive trade show held at the Las Vegas Convention Center in Nevada, and Nissan eagerly joins the party, once again, with a triple concept showcase.
Actually, this trio might only be the appetizer for the Japanese automaker’s North American subsidiary, as the 2026 SEMA Show is still around the corner and the brands might showcase only a few of their stars in advance. So far, we have already seen at least some of the reveals and hints from Dodge, Ford, Toyota, or Mitsubishi, each showcasing their strengths.
Mitsubishi, for example, revealed the 2028 Outlander Diamond Trail Edition ; Toyota has already shown a wacky quintet of SUVs and trucks on snow tracks along with the Crown Signia GT-S Performance Concept; Dodge wants to celebrate 90 years of Mopar with a special package for the Charger fastback coupe, and the Blue Oval is focusing on the Bronco, as far as we can tell.
Now Nissan joins the preview party with a revival of the Sentra Spec-V and two enthusiast-inspired Z concepts, “each offering a fresh take on Nissan performance and the possibilities of personalization.” There will be something for every sports car enthusiast: Z heritage, modern motorsports, as well as the tuner scene.
Nissan has a reserved booth in the Central Hall at the Las Vegas Convention Center, from November 3 through 6, and the headliner is, for sure, the Nissan Sentra Spec-V Concept which revisits the spirit of a beloved sport compact car – the Sentra SE-R arrived in North America 35 years ago and the new concept is “a tribute to the community that made the Sentra SE-R a star of the import car scene.”
While it still appears like a regular Nissan Sentra, the sport compact sedan is now choke full of Nismo parts, featuring a 300-hp build of its 2.0-liter engine thanks to turbocharging, mixed with an upgraded six-speed manual transmission from the Nissan Juke Nismo RS. There are also GT‑R-sourced Brembo brakes, bespoke Nismo coilovers and anti-roll bars, GT‑R-sourced Recaro front seats, and some rad Nismo LM-RS1 alloy wheels to round out the performance enhancements with the 19-inchers.
There’s also a fully custom body kit along with a GT-R Nismo rear spoiler to complete the look, and the car rides on 265/35R19 Yokohama Advan Neova AD09 tires! The first of the two Zs is the Nissan Project NAT2 SCCA Touring 2 sports car, developed in-house by the Nissan Acceleration Team (NAT), an all-volunteer group of employees who play with motorsports in their free time. As the name implies, it was created to comply with SCCA Touring 2 specifications featuring upgrades for the engine, suspension, and braking systems using both Nismo and aftermarket parts.
Last but not least is also a Datsun S30 Concept - Formula Drift champion and Z enthusiast Chris Forsberg, a longtime Nissan collaborator, spins the original Z toward the restomod area with the S30 concept fitting a twin-turbo V6 powertrain from the current Z. There are also Nismo upgrades added to the engine, several major body panels were replaced with lightweight carbon fiber, and there are also unique suspension and braking components.
There’s also a Nissan Z FS6 six-speed manual transmission, a Nismo R200 limited-slip differential, and Garrett PMAX turbochargers; a Nismo 40th decal set mixed with a stunning Nissan Seiran Blue paint; a ton of Techno Toy Tuning components for the suspension, Nismo forged wheels, Wilwood brakes, and a very nice interior featuring OMP Silverstone racing seats and many other things.

VICTORIA, British Columbia — Saab will collaborate with several of Canada’s top aerospace firms to build the Gripen fighter jet in Canada if the aircraft is selected by the Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government.
Saab confirmed Oct. 27 that it has formed alliances with several firms to build, deliver and support the Gripen E advanced multi-role fighter, should the Canadian government purchase the plane.
Canada had already committed to buying 88 Lockheed Martin F-35s but that is under review after U.S. President Donald Trump threatened to economically cripple the country and suggested it could be annexed to be the 51 st state. At this point Canada has paid for 16 F-35s.
Two of the aircraft were transferred to Canada on Oct. 9 and Oct. 22, said Department of National Defence spokeswoman Andrée-Anne Poulin.
Canadian Prime Minister Carney will decide whether the rest of the F-35s will be purchased but he has not indicated when he would announce his decision.
In the meantime, the Canadian government is examining whether it should purchase the Gripen E, either as an alternative to the F-35 or to complement the U.S. fighter jets. Saab has responded by forming a teaming arrangement with Canadian firms CAE of Montreal, Quebec; IMP of Halifax, Nova Scotia; and Magellan Aerospace of Mississauga, Ontario.
“Together with CAE, IMP and Magellan Aerospace we are prepared to establish a strong Canadian industrial ecosystem around Gripen that delivers operational effect, national sovereignty and lasting industrial and technological benefits,” Micael Johansson, President and CEO of Saab, said in a statement Oct. 27.
Saab noted it has signed a teaming agreement with IMP to establish a new final assembly line, for the Gripen fighter in Canada, if Canada decides to acquire the aircraft. IMP will also be responsible for electrical assembly production and in-service support for Canada’s Gripens.
Saab has also signed a new Memorandum of Understanding with Magellan Aerospace to provide local manufacturing of advanced aerostructures, composite structures and structural assemblies in Canada — again, if Canada decides to acquire the aircraft.
Saab has previously signed a Memorandum of Understanding with CAE to deliver advanced fighter pilot and technician training, mission systems engineering and support/sustainment capabilities in Canada.
Saab has already made significant inroads into the Canadian market.
Carney announced May 27 that Canada will purchase six GlobalEye early warning and control aircraft from Saab as part of deal to not only boost Canadian military capabilities but energize domestic defense production.
Carney said the proposed GlobalEye purchase is estimated to cost more than $5 billion CAN ($3.6 billion).
GlobalEye is based on a Bombardier 6500 executive jet, an aircraft that is manufactured in Toronto. Carney said that at least one-third of the projected GlobalEye aircraft orders for various allies will be built in Canada. That is expected to be 40 aircraft over the next 15 years.
On Sept. 25 the Canadian government announced it had worked out an agreement with Saab that will provide the framework for upcoming negotiations on the purchase of the six GlobalEyes.
In announcing the agreement, Stephen Fuhr, Secretary of State for Defence Procurement, said Canada will be focusing on pursuing a partnership that supports “Canadian jobs, innovation, and long-term economic growth while ensuring we acquire capabilities from trusted partners when they are needed.”

By Angelo Mathais India correspondent
28 October 2026
Vessel-handling services have been suspended or restricted across several major ports along India’s east coast since Monday, due to Cyclone Arnab warnings.
The severe storm made landfall on India’s eastern coastline this morning, bringing huge swells and gale winds across the region, according to reports.
One key gateway port that suspended all operations until further notice was Visakhapatnam, a critical feeder port for Maersk’s coverage out of India’s east coast, especially for cargo moving in and out of Kolkata.
Kuehne+Nagel told customers: “Potentially impacted container ports include Visakhapatnam , Gangavaram , and Krishnapatnam , all of which have received cyclone or storm warnings as Arnab approaches India’s east coast.”
Industry sources in India believe the port suspensions could inevitably cause congestion and delays to freight flow, but the scale will only be known when terminals fully reopen.
“Visakhapatnam terminals are slowly getting back to business, in tandem with government guidelines and updates,” one carrier official told The Loadstar . “The ports were told to keep operations suspended as part of contingency planning.”
According to the latest updates, the cyclonic storm claimed three lives in India’s Andhra Pradesh State, in addition to causing extensive damage to residential properties and utility installations in the region.
Several Indian ports had already been experiencing operational pressures due to widespread vessel bunching tied to delayed arrivals from Asian origin ports, and “the cyclone disruption is another blow to the supply chains”, said a Visakhapatnam-based ship agent.
Visakhapatnam handled 302,926 teu year-to-date through September, edging down from 308,861 teu year on year, according to data collected by The Loadstar .
Meanwhile, the authorities in Bangladesh issued similar cautionary alerts for ports as the cyclone threatened gusty weather over the northern Bay of Bengal and adjoining coastal areas.
“Cyclonic Storm Arnab has formed over the east-central and adjoining west-central Bay of Bengal and is forecast to intensify into a very severe cyclonic storm before making landfall along the Andhra Pradesh and Yanam coasts on 28 October,” London-based port agency service provider Inchcape Shipping Services told customers.
Congestion and operational disruption issues are not limited to the Indian coast. K+N also reported an average vessel waiting time of two days across terminals in Sri Lanka’s Colombo port, “due to ongoing transhipment congestion, missed feeder connections, vessel omissions and routing changes”, the company said.

Original Owner, Sons Reunite With 1962 Pontiac Catalina 421 SD He Had New, They Last Saw It in 1972
13 photos
Photo: YouTube/Real World Garage
Pontiac is no more, it died 45 years ago, when the division made its last V8, a 301-cuber, ending a streak of 14,620,000 eight-cylinders cast between 1955 and February 20, 1981. Sure, General Motors kept PMD of life support for another 29 years before pulling the plug for good in 2010. Which was 48 years after Pontiac released one of its most famous powerplants of all time, the incredible, amazing, fabulous 421 Super Duty. This father-sons trio held a special gathering to dad’s former race car he last saw in 1972.
Decades of American drag racing heritage condensed into a sunny afternoon when three members of the Sharp family gathered around a gleaming crimson 1962 Pontiac Catalina Super Duty. Captured by host Brian Gainey on the Real World Garage YouTube channel, the emotional reunion brought octogenarian racer Barney Lewis Sharp together with his sons, William and John, alongside the legendary factory lightweight race car affectionately nicknamed “Big Chief.”
For the trio, this gathering marked the first occasion in 54 years that all three men stood together beside the machine that shaped their family lore. John Sharp flew in from Oregon specifically for the event, having only seen photographs, magazine features, and video clips of the restored Pontiac for more than 50 years. Standing together, the family admired its remarkably authentic factory-fresh condition and finish.
The story of this remarkable automobile began in late 1962 at Lane-Moak Pontiac in Jackson, Mississippi, where dealership co-owner Colin Lane grew tired of an undefeated local 1957 Chevrolet Corvette 283-cubic-inch Fuelie. Determined to humble the sports car, Lane ordered the only 1962 Super Duty delivered in Mississippi and had it shipped directly to Nichels Engineering in Highland, Indiana, where specialists blueprinted the 421-cubic-inch V8 to legal drag racing specifications.
Photo: YouTube/Real World Garage Built as 1 of only 88 factory lightweight Catalinas equipped with aluminum fenders, inner panels, hood, and bumpers that shaved 200 lbs off the curb weight, the 3,850-lb brawler also featured a rare factory cigar lighter requested by mechanic Lewis Sharp. Paired with a close-ratio Borg-Warner 4-speed manual transmission and a 4.30:1 rear axle, the Pontiac easily defeated the rival Corvette, which later won the national B/Stock drag racing championship.
Although the Lane-Moak Catalina had the speed to capture the national crown in Indianapolis, the dealership simply could not afford the travel expenses to enter the finals. Initially, Sharp wrenched on the car while his skeptical brother-in-law served as the designated driver. Ignoring warnings about its violent temperament, the brother-in-law pulled second gear during an early run, spun in a full circle, and slid onto an adjacent dirt oval track.
That terrifying lateral lurch occurred because soft factory rubber bushings in the rear control arms allowed the axle to shift under heavy torque, forcing Sharp to steer hard right whenever he grabbed second gear. His friend Billy “Peanut” Buck joked that spectators at the starting line could see the headlights as Sharp crossed the finish line sideways. After Lane-Moak retired the car in 1964, Sharp bought it for $850.
Photo: YouTube/Real World Garage With the Big Chief moniker painted on the flanks, Sharp campaigned the Pontiac for five seasons until 1969, recording a best elapsed time of 11.88 seconds at Biloxi, Mississippi, and a top speed of 122 mph at Monroe, Louisiana. At Monroe, a bitter rival constantly accused him of running an illegal displacement, so Sharp invited the critic to measure the bare cylinder bores for free before bolting the heads on.
After the rival inspected the factory block, Sharp reassembled the motor and launched wide open, holding the dash tachometer at 6,000 rpm to hit 120 mph through the traps. His stunned accuser admitted he would have demanded an immediate teardown had he not just seen the open engine himself. Throughout those years, Sharp usually took $10 in gas money instead of trophies, giving his hardware away to eager local children.
Rising racing costs forced Sharp to sell the Catalina in 1969, and 15 years later his son spotted it languishing outside a service station in Crystal Springs, Mississippi, for $1,000. Sharp declined to buy it back, opening the door for Ardmore, Oklahoma, restorer Eugene Riotte to acquire the rough hulk in 1987. When Riotte visited Sharp, the former racer generously gifted him the original 1962 dual-quad intake from his shed.
Photo: YouTube/Real World Garage Sharp had removed that manifold years earlier to run a borrowed 1963 dual-quad setup that held the carburetors level, which a thief later stole from his house, taking parts worth $2,500 to $3,000 today. Because the original motor had been sold after 7 races for a dirt tracker, Riotte spent 24 years rebuilding the Catalina with a period-correct high-nickel 421-cubic-inch Super Duty block bored 0.045 inches over to 431 cubic inches.
Fitted with forged internals, 2.02-inch intake and 1.76-inch exhaust stainless steel valves, a 12.25:1 compression ratio, brass rear suspension bushings, and replicated factory chalk marks, the Pontiac debuted in July 2011 in Bowling Green, Kentucky. There, Sharp reunited with the car after 42 years as it scored 400 out of 400 points.
Purchased by Sam Wofford in 2019, the coupe was showcased on several YouTube channels, including automotive chronicler Lou Costabile’s (the second one attached below).
Photo: YouTube/Real World Garage The fearsome reputation of the Big Chief stems from the broader legacy of the Pontiac Super Duty moniker, which spanned from 1960 to 1963 before returning in 1973 and 1974. Introduced in 1960 on the 389-cubic-inch V8 with a single four-barrel or Tri-Power induction producing up to 385 gross hp, the program expanded in late 1961 with the 6.9-liter 421-cubic-inch V8, installed in 155 Catalinas and 16 Grand Prix coupes for 1962.
While 7 additional 1962 Catalinas received the 389-cubic-inch engine, the dual-quad 421-cubic-inch Super Duty V8 was OFFICIALLY rated at 405 hp at 5,600 rpm and 425 lb-ft of torque at 4,400 rpm. Real output sat a lot closer to 465 gross hp at 7,000 rpm, with a torque of about 510 lb-ft.
In 1973 and 1974, Pontiac revived the badge on the 455-cubic-inch Firebird Formula and Trans Am, delivering 310 net hp in 1973 and 290 net hp in 1974.
Photo: YouTube/Real World Garage Early Super Duty cars offered a standard 3-speed manual, an optional Borg-Warner T-10 4-speed manual, or a Roto Hydra-Matic automatic, whereas the 1973 and 1974 models utilized a Muncie 4-speed manual or Turbo Hydra-Matic 400 automatic. Dominating both stock car ovals and drag strips, a showroom-stock 1962 Catalina 421-cubic-inch Super Duty sprinted from 0 to 60 mph in 5.4 seconds and ran the quarter-mile in 13.9 seconds at 107 mph.
In the dead of winter, in 20°F (negative 6°C), on a snow-powdered, unprepped surface, with two grown men aboard, and 150 lb of ballast in the trunk. That’s what Motor Trend scored back in January 1962 (they also calculated the 421 SD’s true output), and estimated that, on a good day, on a good strip, the big Catalina would’ve cleared the quick-quarter in mid 12s, at trap speeds above 115 mph, after the zero-to-hero sprint of 4.5 seconds.
Ordering that factory-engineered velocity back in 1962 demanded a serious financial commitment, as a base Pontiac Catalina coupe carried a sticker price of $2,725 before options. Selecting the complete 421-cubic-inch Super Duty engine and lightweight aluminum body package added more than $2,250 to the invoice, pushing the final price past $5,100.
It was a lot of money, but it bought a die-hard racer bragging rights over everything else on the road back then, from 413 Max Wedges and Chevy 409s to Ford 406s.

The freight industry has spent years and real money chasing fraud, piling up more tracking, more data, and more awareness than it has ever had, and the losses keep climbing anyway, which is the paradox Michael Caney, Chief Customer Officer at the Carrier Identity® platform Highway, set out to unpack at the FreightWaves Broker Compliance Symposium, and his answer began with a reframe most of the room had never sat with, that fraud is not really the problem at all but a signal pointing at a deeper one the industry keeps refusing to name.
Caney, who spent two decades as an operator before moving to the technology side, started from a hard truth. No industry has ever eradicated fraud. He pointed to healthcare, where the total addressable market for fraud keeps growing despite decades of fighting it, and to the fact that none of us have switched off our own credit monitoring because the threat simply does not disappear. Fraud, he argued, is a symptom that tells you where to go look, and the freight business has spent its energy swatting at the symptom instead of treating the condition underneath.
Three Ingredients, And An Industry Full Of Them
Fraud needs three things to work, Caney said, the prospect of gain, anonymity, and urgency, and freight hands criminals an abundance of the last two. A broker under pressure to cover a load before a shipper’s clock runs out is a broker tempted to relax a standard, and a bad actor who can stay anonymous long enough to exploit that urgent moment can steal freight, endanger the motoring public, and move on. The uncomfortable part is that brokers sit at the dead center of this, which Caney framed as either a curse or an opportunity depending on how the industry chooses to respond, with the roughly 600 million dollar broker verdict hanging over the symposium as a reminder of how expensive the curse version gets.
The Problem Is Not Data, It Is Enforceability
Here Caney made his sharpest point. The industry does not actually suffer from a lack of standards. Everyone in the room has standards. What it lacks is standards that are shared, arbitrated, and above all enforceable, and a system where ignoring them carries a consequence. He drove the point home by naming three groups that feed brokers enormous amounts of data while carrying, in his telling, very little accountability, the insurance agents, the telematics providers, and the factoring companies that collect premiums and receivables off the freight transaction yet were nowhere to be found at a compliance symposium. When an insurance agent submits bad data, misses a cancellation, or lets a scheduled item lapse, the broker making a hiring decision on that data is the one left exposed.
The numbers he gave on insurance data alone were striking. Of roughly 10,000 agents feeding the system, he said about 40 cover nearly half the vehicles while 200 cover only 3 percent, which means thousands of small sources push data that brokers rely on for vetting with almost no continuity, timeliness, or accuracy. Having that much data, Caney said, is not the same as being able to enforce anything with it.
Years Of Chasing The Signal
The reason freight is in this spot, he argued, is that it has conditioned itself to run at the signal rather than the source. Something goes missing, something is late, a number is off, and the response is to call a TMS provider or a vendor to fix that one thing, then move to the next one. He walked the room back to the era before load tracking was universal, when shippers began selling the little blue dot for a dollar a load with the promise that all problems would vanish, then pushed the cost onto brokers when carriers balked. Years later the industry tracks almost everything, spends heavily to do it, and still watches fraud rise.
The spending without accountability is its own tell. Caney said that when brokers audit their own technology bills, the tracking line is enormous, built on volume, on pings and searches rather than on outcomes, and yet those same brokers will balk at a 500 dollar fee tied to a guaranteed load. His blunt arithmetic was that 500 dollars is cheaper than 600 million, and that with everything a broker already pours into tracking, the load ought to be on time to begin with.
Verified Data Versus The Data You Think You Have
One of the more pointed moments was about the gap between reported and real performance. Carriers routinely hand over tracking records showing 90 percent compliance, Caney said, and when Highway runs those records through its own verification the true figure often lands closer to 75 percent, exposing chameleon carriers and operators gaming the scorecard. For a long time, meeting a customer’s scorecard on paper was enough to keep the freight flowing, with no consequence for the vendor that oversold the tracking or the carrier that faked it. What has changed, in his framing, is that the industry finally has a stick. Highway will de-certify a telematics provider whose network is riddled with carriers that steal, drop a carrier, or refuse to accept insurance certificates from an agent whose data cannot be trusted.
Risk Has Moved From Rules To Process
Caney’s forward-looking argument was that the industry’s risk has shifted from its rules to its processes. For years brokers believed the answer was better rules, and they accumulated them, one oddly specific exception at a time, until configuring a new rule went from a six-month statement of work to a thirty-minute task. The result, he said, is that brokers now hold more rules than ever and override a huge share of them, so many that the rules are no longer really their own. The future is not more data for its own sake or more rules layered on top, but simpler decisions baked into the workflow, powered by network effects rather than tribal knowledge living in one person’s head.
That is why he kept returning to automation and context. A load, in his view, is becoming less like a truck going from A to B and more like a fully digital financial transaction with many parties contributing to whether it conforms or not. Good vetting should not just confirm a carrier is satisfactory or passes a rule set, it should confirm the carrier actually carries the insurance to haul this specific load, catching the buried policy exceptions, the commodity that is not covered, the liability limit that falls short. None of that, he argued, belongs on a sticky note in a cubicle, and tracking should initiate automatically rather than depending on someone asking a driver to accept an app, because the carriers doing the right thing show up, connect, and are easy to verify, while the ones that resist are the exception worth examining.
A Buttonwood Moment For Freight
Where this goes next, Caney said, is toward guarantees at the transaction level, borrowing the language of lending, where conforming and non-conforming loans became prime and subprime. Highway, he noted, has guaranteed well over a billion dollars in freight and rarely paid out, the exceptions tracing back to someone gaming a certification. But the real close was a call to collective action. He observed that of his 1,500 customers, only 243 had enrolled in the stricter Performance Guarantee standard that costs nothing but requires following the rules, and that those 243 had moved a million loads with what he called total peace of mind, leaving the obvious question of where the other 1,300 were.
To make the stakes plain he reached for history, citing Dee Hock, the founder of Visa, and the warning that an industry that will not govern itself from within will be governed from without. He invoked the Buttonwood Agreement of May 1792 , when a couple dozen brokers standing under a tree on Wall Street agreed on the standards and the conduct that would define their trade and, in doing so, seeded what became the New York Stock Exchange. The lesson he drew was that standards never emerge from a vendor’s successful funding round or a great pitch, they emerge when the participants themselves get together and decide what is acceptable and what is not, and attach consequences to the difference. The companies that come out of the current fraud crisis strongest, he predicted, will be the ones that stop waiting and start setting those requirements for every party in the transaction, from insurance agents to telematics providers to factoring companies.
Why It Matters
Freight does not have a data problem, it has an enforcement problem, and no amount of additional tracking or rule-writing will fix a system where the parties feeding the data face no consequence for feeding it badly. Caney’s challenge to brokers is that the tools to verify carriers, automate vetting, and guarantee loads already exist, so the real variable now is whether the industry will govern itself by agreeing on shared, enforceable standards, or keep chasing the next fraud signal until it is governed from the outside by rules it had no hand in writing.

The Dee Hock and 1792 Buttonwood Agreement references are his, used to frame a call for industry self-governance.
